title: Methods for Automated Equivalence Checking of Quantum Error-Correction Codes
authors: Maxie Bichmann, Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
abstract: Quantum error-correction code and circuit construction is an active field of research, motivating automated methods for identifying equivalent designs. We develop and evaluate automated strategies for deciding whether two descriptions of quantum error-correction codes are equivalent under specified transformations. We formalize permutation equivalence for stabilizer and CSS codes and local-Clifford equivalence for stabilizer codes within a unified framework that separates physical from representation freedom. We develop three decision strategies (group-action search, isomorphism-based methods, and constraint solving), together with invariants and signatures for preprocessing. The empirical evaluation shows that no paradigm dominates across equivalence notions, code families, and parameter ranges. We therefore combine their complementary strengths in input-dependent hybrid checkers following a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture. Mean hybrid runtimes remain below 10 s for most evaluated structured-code cases with $n \leq 37$; for inequivalent code instances with $n=144$, they are about 310 s for permutation and 16 s for local-Clifford equivalence.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of automatically checking if two quantum error-correcting codes are equivalent, accounting for multiple sources of ambiguity. The authors develop and benchmark a hybrid computational framework that combines several advanced techniques to solve this problem efficiently. The work provides a crucial tool for the field by offering scalable, systematic methods for code comparison.
main_problem: The paper develops automated methods to determine if two descriptions of Quantum Error-Correction (QEC) codes are equivalent under various transformations.
main_result: No single algorithmic paradigm works universally, necessitating a hybrid checker combining group-action search, isomorphism methods, and constraint solving for optimal performance.
method: The authors formalize equivalence notions (like permutation and local-Clifford) and combine three distinct algorithmic strategies into a staged Refute-Refine-Decide architecture.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Error-Correction Codes (QECCs), specifically stabilizer codes and CSS codes, which are defined by their generator matrices and associated Pauli group structures.
key_observables: Mean runtimes for equivalence checking, the fraction of distinguished qubit pairs ($ ar{q}$), and the number of SAT solver decisions.
important_parameters: Physical qubit number ($n$), number of stabilizers ($r$), and the specific equivalence notion (permutation vs. local-Clifford).
main_assumptions: The work assumes that the core challenge lies in automating the comparison across different representations and physical freedoms inherent in code descriptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ambiguity of code representations (e.g., Steane code realizations) and compare the runtime and memory scaling of various encoding techniques (Full-Group vs. Matroid-Circuit) for equivalence checking.
paper_structure: The paper systematically defines the problem by separating physical freedom from representation freedom, develops multiple algorithmic tools (group action, isomorphism, constraint solving), and empirically evaluates their combined performance.
why_interesting: While focused on QEC, the rigorous development of automated algebraic and computational tools for determining structural equivalence is highly relevant to characterizing complex quantum states and codes used in quantum simulation.
